Delaware corporations · officer exculpation

QUESTION · DELAWARE CORPORATIONS

Authorities accessed August 17, 2026

Yes, the charter can shield officers from money damages for careless decisions.

Can the charter shield our officers from personal liability?

The reader asked a yes-or-no question, so the title answers it.

Yes, since August 1, 2022. The 2022 amendment to 8 Del. C. §102(b)(7) lets the certificate of incorporation eliminate or limit covered officers' personal liability for money damages for duty-of-care breaches. The charter must say so. The statute gives officers no protection on its own.

Yes, if the charter says so. Since August 1, 2022 a Delaware charter can shield the named officers from money damages for careless decisions (8 Del. C. §102(b)(7)). It cannot shield disloyalty, bad faith, or a suit by the company itself. Putting it in place takes a board resolution, a stockholder vote, and a filing.

States the rule and its source before the limits, for a reader who wants the legal basis first.

What the shield covers, and what it never covers.

8 Del. C. §102(b)(7), accessed August 17, 2026.

Enclosure shows what sits inside the shield and what never can. The charter line is the crossing.

Which claims and officers can it cover?

A charter provision can reach direct stockholder claims seeking money damages from an officer for a duty-of-care breach. It limits that remedy; it does not erase the duty. 8 Del. C. §102(b)(7)

"Officer" means the president, CEO, COO, CFO, chief legal officer, controller, treasurer, or chief accounting officer; an executive identified as one of the most highly compensated in SEC filings; or a person who agreed in writing to be treated as an officer for this purpose. 10 Del. C. §3114(b)

Who and what it covers.

Claims: a stockholder's direct claim for money damages over a careless decision. The duty stays; the damages remedy goes. 8 Del. C. §102(b)(7)

Officers: the president, CEO, COO, CFO, chief legal officer, controller, treasurer, and chief accounting officer; an executive named among the most highly compensated in SEC filings; anyone who agreed in writing to be treated as an officer. 10 Del. C. §3114(b)

Answers the question the reader will ask first, in the order the statute states it.

How does the corporation adopt it?

First, the board adopts a resolution that sets out the amendment and declares it advisable. The proposal then goes to the stockholders for the required vote. After approval, the corporation executes and files a certificate of amendment. 8 Del. C. §242(b)(1)

The amendment is effective when filed unless it states a permitted later effective time. 8 Del. C. §103(d)

The board must act first. The corporation cannot begin with a stockholder vote.

Three steps, in this order.

  1. The board adopts a resolution that sets out the amendment and declares it advisable.
  2. The stockholders vote to approve it. 8 Del. C. §242(b)(1)
  3. The corporation files a certificate of amendment. It takes effect on filing unless it names a later time, at most 90 days out. 8 Del. C. §103(d)

The board must act first.

Prose keeps the three acts and the effective-time rule in one reading.

What can it never cover?

The statute always leaves officers exposed for breaches of the duty of loyalty; acts or omissions not in good faith; intentional misconduct; knowing violations of law; and transactions from which the officer received an improper personal benefit. 8 Del. C. §102(b)(7)(i), (ii), (iv)

Unlike directors, officers also stay exposed in actions brought by the corporation or in its right, so derivative claims stay live against officers. 8 Del. C. §102(b)(7)(v)

The provision cannot reach an act or omission that happened before it took effect.

Derivative claims stay live, and so do five kinds of conduct.

Unlike directors, officers stay exposed to claims brought by the corporation or in its right. A derivative suit over the same careless decision is not shielded. 8 Del. C. §102(b)(7)(v)

The provision also never covers loyalty breaches, bad faith, intentional misconduct, knowing violations of law, or an improper personal benefit. 8 Del. C. §102(b)(7)(i), (ii), (iv)

Nothing before the effective date is covered.

Lists the exclusions in the statute's own order so counsel can check them against the text.

Why would a board do it?

It can put officers closer to directors on protection from money claims over careless decisions, reducing a gap that can complicate executive recruiting and retention.

It also changes settlement pressure. A care claim dismissed against exculpated directors could otherwise continue against officers on the same facts.

The amendment narrows one damages remedy. It does not protect loyalty breaches, bad faith, improper benefits, or derivative claims against officers.

Why boards do it.

Two reasons. It closes most of the gap between director and officer protection, which matters when recruiting and keeping executives. It removes the pressure of a care claim that was dismissed against the directors but continues against the officers on the same facts.

One limit. It narrows a single damages remedy and nothing else.

The fuller register, for a reader who wants the reasoning before the recommendation.

Next step. The board adopts the resolution. The stockholder vote and the filing follow from it.

Your decision. Whether to put the resolution on the next board agenda, and which officers the provision should name.

Names the single act that starts the process.

This page addresses a Delaware stock corporation adding officer exculpation to its certificate of incorporation. It is not legal advice. It reflects the Delaware Code accessed August 17, 2026 and does not analyze a particular charter, class-vote requirement, claim, or officer.

Covered · 8 Del. C. §102(b)(7)

What a covered suit alleges

A stockholder sues the officer directly for money, claiming a decision was careless — that the officer acted without enough information or attention and so breached the duty of care. With the charter provision in place, the officer does not pay personal monetary damages on that claim. The duty itself remains; the shield removes only the damages remedy.

§102(b) (7) A provision eliminating or limiting the personal liability of a director or officer to the corporation or its stockholders for monetary damages for breach of fiduciary duty…

Never covered · §102(b)(7)(i), (iv)

What a disloyalty suit alleges

The claim is that the officer put personal interest ahead of the corporation — self-dealing, taking a corporate opportunity, or receiving an improper personal benefit. That alleges a breach of the duty of loyalty, and the statute does not let a charter shield it.

Delaware Code, title 8, ch. 1, subch. I, §102(b)(7) — the grant and carve-outs (i)–(v) (official online code).

Never covered · §102(b)(7)(ii)

What a bad-faith suit alleges

The claim is that the officer acted in bad faith — intentional misconduct, a knowing violation of law, or acts or omissions not in good faith. Carelessness can be shielded; knowing wrongdoing cannot.

Delaware Code, title 8, ch. 1, subch. I, §102(b)(7) — the grant and carve-outs (i)–(v) (official online code).

Never covered · §102(b)(7)(v)

What a corporate or derivative suit alleges

Here the corporation is the plaintiff — directly, or through a stockholder suing on its behalf in a derivative claim. The provision blocks only direct stockholder claims for money; claims by or in the right of the corporation stay live against officers.

8 Del. C. §102(b)(7)

What an officer-exculpation provision may—and may not—do

The certificate may eliminate or limit a covered officer’s personal liability to the corporation or its stockholders for monetary damages for fiduciary breach. The text excludes loyalty breaches, bad faith, intentional misconduct, knowing law violations, improper personal benefit, claims by or in the right of the corporation against an officer, and conduct predating the provision.

§102(b) (7) A provision eliminating or limiting the personal liability of a director or officer to the corporation or its stockholders for monetary damages for breach of fiduciary duty…

Delaware Code, title 8, ch. 1, subch. I, §102(b)(7) — the grant and carve-outs (i)–(v) (official online code).

83 Del. Laws, c. 377, §§1, 21

The 2022 amendment that added officers

Section 1 amended §102(b)(7) to add officers while preserving officer-specific exclusions, including claims by or in the right of the corporation. Section 21 made that change effective August 1, 2022.

Section 21: “Sections 1 through 8, Section 10, Sections 12 through 14, and Sections 16 through 20 shall be effective on August 1, 2022.”

83 Del. Laws, c. 377, §§1, 21 (S.B. 273, 151st Gen. Assem.; approved July 27, 2022; §102(b)(7) amendment effective Aug. 1, 2022).

Which officers fall within the statutory cross-reference

The list covers eight named offices, executives identified as among the most highly compensated in SEC filings, and people who agree in writing to be treated as officers for this section. §102(b)(7) imports that list to define which officers may be exculpated.

8 Del. C. §242(b)(1)

The board resolution, stockholder vote, and certificate

For a stock corporation, the board first adopts a resolution setting out the amendment and declaring it advisable, then calls a stockholder meeting. After the required stockholder approval, a certificate of amendment is executed and filed.

A certificate setting forth the amendment and certifying that such amendment has been duly adopted… shall be executed, acknowledged and filed and shall become effective in accordance with § 103 of this title.

Delaware Code, title 8, ch. 1, subch. VIII, §242(b) chapeau and §242(b)(1) (official online code).

8 Del. C. §103(d)

When the filed amendment becomes effective

A filed instrument is effective on its filing date unless it specifies a later effective time. That later time cannot be more than 90 days after filing.

Any instrument filed in accordance with subsection (c) of this section shall be effective upon its filing date…

Delaware Code, title 8, ch. 1, subch. I, §103(d) (official online code).
